problem_statement:
*** Problem Statement ***

Consider a $2025\times2025$ grid of unit squares. Matilda wishes to place on the grid some rectangular tiles, possibly of difference sizes, such that each side of every tile lies on a grid line and every unit square is covered by at most one tile.

Determine the minimum number of tiles Matilda needs to place so that each row and each column of the grid has exactly one unit square that is not covered by any tile.
solution:
### Summary ###

**a. Verdict:** I have found a complete solution.  
The minimum number of tiles required is  

\[
\boxed{2025}.
\]

**b. Method Sketch:**  

1. **Encoding the uncovered squares.**  
   Choose a permutation \(\sigma\) of \(\{1,\dots ,n\}\) (\(n=2025\)).  
   The unique uncovered square in row \(i\) is \((i,\sigma(i))\).  

2. **Matrix formulation.**  
   Let \(J\) be the \(n\times n\) all‑ones matrix and let \(P_{\sigma}\) be the permutation matrix of \(\sigma\).  
   Define  

   \[
   M:=J-P_{\sigma},
   \tag{1}
   \]

   so that \(M_{ij}=1\) exactly for the squares that must be covered.

3. **Tiles ↔ rank‑1 Boolean matrices.**  
   A rectangular tile covering a set of rows \(R\subseteq\{1,\dots ,n\}\) and columns \(C\subseteq\{1,\dots ,n\}\) corresponds to the Boolean matrix  

   \[
   A_{RC}=u_Rv_C^{\mathsf T},
   \tag{2}
   \]

   where \(u_R\) (resp. \(v_C\)) is the indicator column vector of \(R\) (resp. \(C\)).  
   Condition that the tile avoids uncovered squares is  

   \[
   C\cap\sigma(R)=\varnothing .
   \tag{3}
   \]

   Hence a family of tiles covering all 1‑entries of \(M\) is precisely a Boolean decomposition  

   \[
   M=\bigvee_{t=1}^{k}u_{R_t}v_{C_t}^{\mathsf T},
   \tag{4}
   \]

   where \(\bigvee\) denotes entrywise logical OR.  
   The smallest possible \(k\) equals the **Boolean rank** of \(M\).

4. **Lower bound via real rank.**  
   For any Boolean matrix, its real (ordinary) rank does not exceed its Boolean rank.  
   Therefore  

   \[
   \operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb R}(M)\le\text{Boolean rank}(M).
   \tag{5}
   \]

   We compute \(\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb R}(M)=n\).  
   Indeed, \(M\mathbf{1}= (n-1)\mathbf{1}\) (where \(\mathbf{1}\) is the all‑ones vector) and for any vector \(x\) orthogonal to \(\mathbf{1}\) we have \(Jx=0\), so  

   \[
   Mx = -P_{\sigma}x .
   \]

   Since every eigenvalue \(\lambda\) of the permutation matrix \(P_{\sigma}\) satisfies \(|\lambda|=1\) and \(\lambda\neq0\), the restriction of \(M\) to the subspace \(\mathbf{1}^{\perp}\) is invertible (its eigenvalues are \(-\lambda\neq0\)).  
   Hence \(M\) is nonsingular, implying \(\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb R}(M)=n\).

   Combining (5) with this gives  

   \[
   \text{Boolean rank}(M)\ge n .
   \tag{6}
   \]

   Consequently at least \(n\) tiles are necessary.

5. **Construction with \(n\) tiles.**  
   For each column \(j\) place the vertical tile  

   \[
   R_j=\{1,\dots ,n\}\setminus\{\sigma^{-1}(j)\},\qquad C_j=\{j\}.
   \]

   This tile covers all squares of column \(j\) except the uncovered square \((\sigma^{-1}(j),j)\).  
   The \(n\) tiles are pairwise disjoint (different columns) and together cover every 1‑entry of \(M\).  
   Hence  

   \[
   \text{minimum number of tiles}\le n .
   \tag{7}
   \]

6. **Conclusion.**  
   From (6) and (7) we obtain equality: the minimum number of tiles equals \(n=2025\).  

7. **Remark on “one = 0”.**  
   The problem requires **exactly one** uncovered unit square in each row and each column.  
   Setting the number of uncovered squares per row (and column) to \(0\) violates this requirement; therefore the configuration with no uncovered squares does **not** satisfy the constraints.

---

### Detailed Solution ###

Let \(n=2025\).  
For each row \(i\in\{1,\dots ,n\}\) let the unique uncovered unit square be \((i,\sigma(i))\), where \(\sigma\) is a permutation of \(\{1,\dots ,n\}\).  
Thus the set of uncovered squares is  

\[
U=\{(i,\sigma(i))\mid i=1,\dots ,n\}.
\tag{8}
\]

All other unit squares must be covered by rectangular tiles whose sides lie on grid lines, and no two tiles may overlap.

---

#### 1.  Matrix representation

Define the \(n\times n\) binary matrix  

\[
M_{ij}=
\begin{cases}
0,& j=\sigma(i),\\[2mm]
1,& j\neq\sigma(i).
\end{cases}
\tag{9}
\]

Equivalently, \(M=J-P_{\sigma}\), where  

- \(J\) is the all‑ones matrix \((J_{ij}=1\ \forall i,j)\);  
- \(P_{\sigma}\) is the permutation matrix of \(\sigma\) \(((P_{\sigma})_{ij}=1\iff j=\sigma(i))\).

A tile that covers rows \(R\subseteq\{1,\dots ,n\}\) and columns \(C\subseteq\{1,\dots ,n\}\) covers exactly the entries \((i,j)\) with \(i\in R,\ j\in C\).  
Its indicator matrix is  

\[
A_{RC}=u_Rv_C^{\mathsf T},
\tag{10}
\]

where  

\[
(u_R)_i=
\begin{cases}
1,&i\in R,\\
0,&i\notin R,
\end{cases}
\qquad
(v_C)_j=
\begin{cases}
1,&j\in C,\\
0,&j\notin C.
\end{cases}
\]

Thus \(A_{RC}\) is a rank‑1 Boolean matrix.  
The tile must avoid all uncovered squares, i.e.

\[
C\cap\sigma(R)=\varnothing .
\tag{11}
\]

Consequently a family of tiles \(\{(R_t,C_t)\}_{t=1}^{k}\) covers precisely the 1‑entries of \(M\) iff

\[
M=\bigvee_{t=1}^{k}u_{R_t}v_{C_t}^{\mathsf T},
\tag{12}
\]

where \(\bigvee\) denotes entrywise logical OR.  
The smallest possible \(k\) is the **Boolean rank** of \(M\); it equals the minimal number of tiles required.

---

#### 2.  Lower bound via real rank

For any Boolean matrix \(B\), its real rank \(\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb R}(B)\) does not exceed its Boolean rank.  
Indeed, if \(B=\bigvee_{t=1}^{k}u_t v_t^{\mathsf T}\) with binary vectors \(u_t,v_t\), then the real matrix  

\[
S=\sum_{t=1}^{k}u_t v_t^{\mathsf T}
\tag{13}
\]

has rank at most \(k\) (it is a sum of \(k\) rank‑1 matrices) and satisfies  

\[
B_{ij}=1\iff S_{ij}>0 .
\tag{14}
\]

Since setting positive entries of a real matrix to \(1\) cannot increase its rank, we obtain \(\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb R}(B)\le k\).  
Hence

\[
\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb R}(M)\le\text{Boolean rank}(M).
\tag{15}
\]

We now compute \(\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb R}(M)\).

*Lemma.* The matrix \(M=J-P_{\sigma}\) is nonsingular; therefore \(\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb R}(M)=n\).

*Proof.* Let \(\mathbf{1}\) denote the all‑ones column vector.  
We have \(J\mathbf{1}=n\mathbf{1}\) and \(P_{\sigma}\mathbf{1}=\mathbf{1}\); hence  

\[
M\mathbf{1}=(J-P_{\sigma})\mathbf{1}=(n-1)\mathbf{1}.
\tag{16}
\]

Thus \(\mathbf{1}\) is an eigenvector of \(M\) with eigenvalue \(n-1\neq0\).

Consider any vector \(x\) orthogonal to \(\mathbf{1}\) (i.e. \(\mathbf{1}^{\mathsf T}x=0\)).  
For such \(x\), \(Jx=0\) because each entry of \(Jx\) equals the sum of the components of \(x\).  
Hence  

\[
Mx = -P_{\sigma}x .
\tag{17}
\]

Since \(P_{\sigma}\) is a permutation matrix, its eigenvalues are complex roots of unity; in particular none of them equals \(0\).  
Therefore the restriction of \(M\) to the subspace \(\mathbf{1}^{\perp}\) is invertible (its eigenvalues are \(-\lambda\) where \(\lambda\) runs over the eigenvalues of \(P_{\sigma}\) on \(\mathbf{1}^{\perp}\), all of which satisfy \(|\lambda|=1\)).  
Consequently the only vector satisfying \(Mx=0\) is \(x=0\).  
Thus \(M\) is nonsingular and \(\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb R}(M)=n\). ∎

Combining the lemma with (15) yields

\[
\text{Boolean rank}(M)\ge n .
\tag{18}
\]

Hence any covering of the required squares needs at least \(n\) tiles.

---

#### 3.  Construction using exactly \(n\) tiles

For each column \(j\in\{1,\dots ,n\}\) define  

\[
R_j=\{1,2,\dots ,n\}\setminus\{\sigma^{-1}(j)\},\qquad C_j=\{j\}.
\tag{19}
\]

Because \(\sigma^{-1}(j)\notin R_j\), condition (11) holds, so the pair \((R_j,C_j)\) determines a legal tile: a vertical rectangle of size \((n-1)\times1\) covering column \(j\) except the uncovered square \((\sigma^{-1}(j),j)\).  

The \(n\) tiles \(\{(R_j,C_j)\}_{j=1}^{n}\) are pairwise disjoint (they occupy distinct columns) and together cover every entry \((i,j)\) with \(j\neq\sigma(i)\), i.e. all 1‑entries of \(M\).  
Thus a covering with \(n\) tiles exists, establishing

\[
\text{minimum number of tiles}\le n .
\tag{20}
\]

---

#### 4.  Minimality

From (18) and (20) we have  

\[
\text{minimum number of tiles}=n=2025 .
\tag{21}
\]

---

#### 5.  Comment on the “one = 0” scenario

The problem explicitly demands **exactly one** uncovered unit square in each row and each column.  
Choosing zero uncovered squares per row (and per column) would violate this requirement; consequently a configuration with no uncovered squares does **not** satisfy the constraints.

---

Hence the minimal number of rectangular tiles needed is \(\boxed{2025}\).

---
